chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ruled regarding your blood (blood money/diyyah) differently from how He ruled regarding your wealth. He ruled regarding your wealth that the evidence is upon the claimant and the oath is upon the one against whom it is claimed. And He ruled regarding your blood that the evidence is upon the one against whom it is claimed and the oath is upon the one who claimed, so that the blood of a Muslim man is not nullified.

key_terms.دَمُ امْرِئٍ مُسْلِمٍ: The blood/life of a Muslim man
key_terms.دِمَائِكُمْ: Your blood (referring to blood money/diyyah compensation)
key_terms.لِكَيْلَا يُبْطَلَ: So that it is not nullified/lost

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in burden of proof between financial claims and blood money (diyyah) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a critical jurisprudential distinction where the burden of proof in diyyah (blood money) cases rests on the defendant, contrasting with the standard 'claimant provides evidence' rule in financial disputes. This inversion serves the higher objective of preserving life by minimizing the risk of wrongful execution or compensation, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on caution in matters of blood. The principle underscores the gravity of taking a life compared to property, ensuring that doubt favors the accused.
